reason: Start with the gear mechanism to see how its parts explain the arm’s motion.

reaction: The concrete wheel-and-rod example made the mechanism clear.
reason: Compare the mechanical approach with feeding, growth and repair before turning to circulation.
expectation: I expect the comparison to raise questions about whether matter and motion can explain these living functions.

alternatives.reason: Heart and valve observations address the remaining circulation goal directly, but the comparison with living functions follows naturally from the mechanism.

effect: The comparison distinguishes imitating movement from explaining living functions; circulation remains to be examined.

reason: Use the only offered combination to investigate how blood returns to the heart.
expectation: I expect the heart and valve observations to show how blood flows back toward the heart.

effect: The circulation account connects arterial outflow with venous return while identifying the unseen tissue connections as a remaining gap.
reaction: The valve observation made the direction of return clear, and the acknowledged gap was useful.

mostWorthwhile.text: The circulation combination was most worthwhile: it linked observations to an explanatory account without concealing what Harvey could not yet see.

leastWorthwhile.text: The gear example was clear but relatively predictable; the later comparison with living functions gave it more depth.

surprise.text: The circulation account could join the two directions of blood flow even though the tiny connections through tissues were not yet visible.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though the offered combinations guided the sequence rather than requiring me to discover compatibility.

continue.text: Yes, I would continue: the contrast between imitating movement and explaining living functions raised an interesting question about the reach of mechanisms.
